column1: # .zap/rules.tsv
# Format: <Rule ID>\t<Threshold>\t# comment
# Threshold: IGNORE | INFO | WARN | FAIL
# IMPORTANT: Run the first scan with this file nearly empty (as it is
# now) and actually read the generated report/GitHub Issue before
# adding anything here. Pre-suppressing alerts you haven't seen yet
# defeats the point of running the scan — you'd be guessing which
# findings are noise instead of knowing. Only add a rule ID here after:
#   1. It fired in a real scan,
#   2. You've read what it actually means, and
#   3. You've concluded it's a genuine false positive or acceptable
#      risk for this app — not just "it's annoying."
# A few near-universal, well-understood entries to start with —
# these are standard for any modern SPA-style Next.js app and are
# informational, not security findings:

column3: # "Modern Web Application" — informational note that the app is a JS-heavy SPA; not a vulnerability.
# "Session Management Response Identified" — informational, not a finding.

column1: # Do NOT add entries here for these common real findings without fixing
# the underlying issue first — they're genuinely worth fixing, not
# suppressing:
#   10035  Strict-Transport-Security Header Not Set
#   10038  Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set
#   10020  X-Frame-Options Header Not Set / Missing Anti-clickjacking Header
#   10021  X-Content-Type-Options Header Missing
#   10054  Cookie without SameSite Attribute
# If any of these fire, the right fix is adding the header/cookie flag
# in next.config.js or middleware.ts — see the headers() config option —
# not silencing the alert.
